7.0.s.en: (1) The settling of the ark and the repentance of the people

7.0.1.en: The people of the village of Kirjath Jearim responded to the request of the people of Beth Shemesh, and went and took the ark and moved it to their city. With reverence they placed the ark in the house of a Levite man named "Abinadab," whose house was on a high place above the village or city. In honor of the ark, "Eleazar" the son of Abinadab was consecrated and set apart to watch over and serve the ark and to prevent anyone from approaching it. It is noted that the people of Kirjath Jearim were distinguished from the people of Beth Shemesh in the following:

7.0.2.en: 1- They did not lift the coverings and did not look at the ark.

7.0.3.en: 2- They set apart a place for the ark hidden from sight and did not leave it on a rock in a field.

7.0.4.en: 3- They set apart a man to watch and guard it and to keep the people from approaching it, and for all this God did not punish them as He punished the people who dared to look at the ark at Beth Shemesh.

7.0.5.en: It is noted that "Abinadab" the Levite man cared for the ark and its service, while the priests neglected to honor the ark and move it to the tabernacle of meeting. The ark remained about 100 years in the house of Abinadab, and Samuel did not concern himself with moving the ark because he was occupied with calling the people to repent of their sins and hold fast to God's commandments, for he cared for the essence of worship before its form. This shows how far the people had declined spiritually and their need to repent first and only afterward offer complete worship to God, that is, their worship was incomplete because the ark was not in the tabernacle.

7.1.1.en: Twenty years passed with the ark settled in Kirjath Jearim, and they were hard years for Israel, in which the Philistines humiliated and oppressed them. So Israel returned to the Lord with weeping and mourning over their sins that had brought them into all this, and thus Samuel's ministry bore fruit in the collective repentance of the people. The ark continued in Kirjath Jearim after that for more than 50 years until King David moved it to Jerusalem (1 Chr 13:3, ch. 15).

7.2.0.en: The Ashtoreths: female pagan goddesses, the plural of Ashtoreth. Ashtoreth was the wife of the god Baal, and adultery was among the rites of her worship.

7.2.1.en: Samuel, the spiritual servant, seized the opportunity of the people's state, their mourning and their desire to return to God, and spoke to all the people, saying: If you truly want to return to God with all your hearts, you must first cleanse your hearts and your houses of the strange gods that crept in among you, which you took from the nations and worshipped with the God of Israel, and you must also prepare your hearts with repentance for the one God, the Holy One of Israel. Then God will look upon you with an eye of mercy and accept you and help you and give you victory over the Philistines, for the worship of God cannot be mixed with the worship of idols, and we cannot keep sin together with the worship of God, but we must cut ourselves off from sin and keep away from it, or else our worship will become formal and without value.

7.3.0.en: Baal: a word meaning "master or lord," applied to the pagan gods, to the male god, and its plural is Baalim.

7.3.1.en: The people responded to Samuel's words, and indeed they removed all the pagan gods from among them, whether the statues of Baal or the Ashtoreths, and returned with all their hearts to the God of Israel.

7.4.0.en: Mizpah: a city lying in the middle of the lands of the tribes, which everyone could easily reach, and lying eight miles north of Jerusalem.

7.4.1.en: Samuel also asked the people to gather in the town of Mizpah, which lies in the land of the tribe of Benjamin, in order to stand with them before God and pray for them, so that God might forgive them their sins.

7.4.2.en: How beautiful is this scene in which Samuel stands between God and His people, praying with them to bring them near to God .. Is this not the very scene of the Divine Liturgy, in which the priest stands between the people and God to present them to Him and to present the Holy God to them, that is, His most holy Body and Blood? Beloved, how can you miss attending the Divine Liturgy from its beginning, so that your heart may be lifted to God and you may be worthy in the end to receive the greatest thing in the world, the sacrament of Communion?..!

7.5.0.en: They drew water: they filled their jars with water.

7.5.1.en: The people of Israel gathered at Mizpah as Samuel had asked. They filled their vessels with water and poured it out before the Lord, as an offering pointing to the pouring out of the heart before God and submission to Him. They also offered an ascetic fast as an expression of their repentance, and acknowledged to Samuel their faults against the Holy One of Israel.

7.5.2.en: After that Samuel stayed for a time at Mizpah, ruling, judging and guiding the people in their questions, their complaints and their various affairs.

7.5.3.en: From this appears the role of Samuel, which was:

7.5.4.en: 1- A spiritual leader leading the people to repentance.

7.5.5.en: 2- A priest who accepts their repentance.

7.5.6.en: 3- A judge who decides their problems according to God's Law.

7.5.7.en: 4- His strength depended on God, therefore he constantly lifted up prayer for his people, for God is the one who protects His people and their true leader.

7.6.0.en: The Philistines heard the news of the gathering of the children of Israel with Samuel at Mizpah, perhaps through spies or through some commercial dealings, since the enmity between the two peoples did not prevent their dealings in buying and selling. Because the Philistines were anxious about this gathering, they sent some of their leaders to Israel to verify the matter, and when the Israelites saw these Philistines they were very afraid and went quickly to their judge Samuel, asking him to pray earnestly to God that He would grant them salvation and victory over the Philistines.

7.6.1.en: Here appears the virtue of the people in the following:

7.6.2.en: 1- Their turning to God, their Savior and Deliverer from the enemies.

7.6.3.en: 2- Their faith in the intercession of Samuel, their spiritual leader.

7.6.4.en: This did not happen the first time at Aphek, therefore they were defeated before the Philistines.

7.7.0.en: Samuel responded to the people's cry and approached God, taking with him a lamb to offer as a burnt offering, that is, to burn it entirely on the altar (Lev 1). After he offered the sacrifice he prayed a fervent prayer, which the inspired text describes as a crying out, and the Lord heard and accepted the sacrifice and prayer of Samuel. The burnt offering is offered entirely to God as a symbol of the consecration of the whole person to God and the obtaining of His favor, just as Christ offered His life on the Cross to please the Father so that He might be pleased with our race.

7.7.1.en: Samuel offered a sacrifice although he was a Levite and not a priest. This was with God's permission because of the special circumstances through which His people were passing, of spiritual decline and the priests' neglect of their office.

7.7.2.en: Prayer is the best spiritual work a person does, and crying out means that the prayer is from the depth of the heart. The people prayed and also asked for the prayer of the man of God on their behalf; you too do likewise. Cry out to God in your affliction and ask those around you in the Church to cry out with you, especially your father the priest, and God will hear and answer.

7.8.0.en: While Samuel was offering his sacrifice, the Philistines gathered to fight the people of God, but God "thundered" upon them. The word thundered may mean one of two things: the first, a figure for God's intervention, who struck terror into the hearts of the Philistines, and the second, that God in reality commanded nature, so that real thunder occurred, very severe and resounding, which unsettled the hearts of the Philistines and made them flee and retreat before Israel. The divine thunder represents the work of grace that supported the men of Israel in their war with the Philistines, which represents spiritual striving, and by the two they triumphed over the Philistines, who fled before them.

7.9.0.en: Beth Car: a Hebrew word meaning house of lambs, and it is a village lying near Mizpah. The Philistines were thrown into confusion and began to withdraw, and the children of Israel followed them to a village called "Beth Car" and beyond, until the Philistines fled completely.

7.10.0.en: As for Samuel, the faithful servant, he did not forget what God had done with the people, and for this reason he wanted to make a memorial that would always be before the people. So he took a stone and set it up between the city of Mizpah and a village called "Shen," and he called this memorial "Ebenezer" (the stone of help), making clear the reason for this name, which was God's help to the people that ended in the defeat of the Philistines before them.

7.11.0.en: Whereas the Philistines had been going in and out of all the lands of the children of Israel in all their arrogance, the hand of the Lord was now against them, and He allowed their humiliation after their haughtiness and pride. This state continued all the days of the prophet Samuel, the man of prayer, who cared for the shepherding of his people, so they lived in the fear of God.

7.12.0.en: The Amorites: among the strongest of the Canaanite peoples, and they dwelt here west of the Jordan, while in the days of Moses they also dwelt east of the Jordan, and he triumphed over them and over their two kings Sihon and Og (Num 21:

7.12.1.en: 21-25.) Israel was able to recover all the small cities lying between the large Philistine cities (Ekron and Gath) which the Philistines had previously occupied, and when the Amorites saw Israel's victory over the Philistines, they sought a peace treaty with Israel, so the days of Samuel were also full of peace with all the neighbors.

7.13.0.en: Bethel: it lies east of Jerusalem and west of Nablus, and it is the first place where Abraham, the father of the fathers, stayed when he entered Canaan.

7.13.1.en: Gilgal: near Jericho, and it was a political and military center in the days of Joshua.

7.13.2.en: Mizpah: in the land of the tribe of Benjamin, lying in a central place of the land of Israel.

7.13.3.en: Samuel was the last of the judges of the people of Israel before they afterward had kings like the rest of the nations. The days of Samuel's service as a judge were blessed days for the people, in which he spared no effort, visiting all the people and going from place to place to judge for them, solve their problems and guide them. The text mentions here the most important stations and centers to which he went every year so that the people could find him.

7.14.0.en: The permanent residence that Samuel took for himself was Ramah (ch. 1:1), where he built an altar after God had established him as priest and accepted his sacrifices ... As for the tabernacle, the morning and evening offerings were offered in it as usual in the city of Shiloh, but the people turned away from it, especially after the ark remained in the town of Kirjath Jearim, and they regarded Samuel as the true priest and leader. Although there was a high priest, most likely Ahitub (ch. 14:3), who followed Eli the priest, all the eyes of the people were toward Samuel the priest and their true leader.

7.14.1.en: It is noted here that there are some exceptions to the rule, which is offering sacrifices only before the house of the Lord, for Samuel offered them in Ramah as he offered a burnt offering at Mizpah (v. 9). For the people were passing through unusual circumstances: they had neglected to return the ark to the house of the Lord at Shiloh and left it in the village of Kirjath Jearim, and thus the tabernacle of meeting at Shiloh was without the ark.

7.14.2.en: In proportion to your prayers and your care for those around you, God intervenes and keeps you and those with you and shepherds you with His fatherhood. So do not neglect prayer and concern for the salvation of the souls of those around you, whether you are small or great, for God works through all.

7.14.3.en: The demand for a king (1) The corruption of Samuel's sons (vv. 1-5:) 1 And it came to pass, when Samuel was old, that he made his sons judges over Israel. 2 Now the name of his firstborn was Joel; and the name of his second, Abiah: they were judges in Beersheba. 3 And his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment. 4 Then all the elders of Israel gathered themselves together, and came to Samuel unto Ramah, 5 And said unto him, Behold, thou art old, and thy sons walk not in thy ways: now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.

8.0.0.en: Samuel used to go about the land of the Jews and judge for them, and when he advanced in days he appointed his two sons Joel and Abiah at Beersheba in the south of Judea to help him in judging the people. It seems that they were distinguished in their character, so the people chose them and Samuel appointed them, and they did not receive this office by inheritance. Samuel had reached the age of about seventy years, that is, about twenty years passed between the previous chapter and this chapter. Samuel judged at Ramah, which lies in the north, while his sons were at Beersheba, which lies in the south, and this shows that there were no wars with the Philistines and consequently there was calm and stability among the tribes of Israel.

8.0.1.en: Near the end of Samuel's life and his judging of the people, we come to the end of the age of the judges, and we shall find that the people will ask for a king, that is, they will enter a new age, the age of the monarchy.

8.1.0.en: But his sons did not walk as their father walked and did not put the fear of God in their hearts, so they turned aside after the desire of the love of money and accepted bribes, and their judgments for the people became unjust, since they looked to their own interests and not the interest of the people. Perhaps this teaches us the necessity of spiritual follow-up with our children, and perhaps this is the only error into which Samuel fell, that he did not follow his sons in their course and their work. For recognizing the fault at its beginning and warning against it is better than slackness and waiting, which makes it a disease that is hard to cure.

8.1.1.en: It may seem strange that Samuel did not profit from the error of Eli the priest, so that corruption also appeared in the two sons of Samuel. But we notice that there are differences between the sin of Eli and that of Samuel in the raising of their sons, so God allowed the death of Eli and his two sons and did not allow it in the case of Samuel and his two sons, for the following reasons:

8.1.2.en: 1- The two sons of Eli the priest were priests and were doing evil in the temple in front of their father, whereas the two sons of Samuel were judging in another place, Beersheba, far from the place where their father lived, which was Ramah.

8.1.3.en: 2- The sin of the two sons of Eli was violent, namely adultery and theft by compulsion.

8.1.4.en: 3- The two sons of Samuel were good and the people chose them, then they erred, and Samuel agreed to their submission to the king and their being tried for any errors into which they fell (1 Sam 12:2).

8.2.0.en: The matter greatly displeased the people, so the leaders of the people gathered and went to Ramah, the permanent residence of the prophet Samuel, and confronted him with the actions of his sons, and how they had turned aside and not walked like him. The surprise that Samuel had not expected at all was that the elders of the people demanded that he appoint a king for them to rule and judge like the rest of the peoples and nations around them.

8.2.1.en: The evident sin of Eli the priest was his laxity with his two sons, who were committing adultery and robbing the people.

8.2.2.en: The strange thing is that despite the holiness of the prophet Samuel, he was lax in the raising of his two sons, so they took bribes when they became judges, which drove the people to an error, namely demanding a king, forgetting God their King.

8.2.3.en: May you learn from the errors of others lest you fall into the same sin, and do not judge them lest you be judged; but hold yourself to account and examine your life carefully and seek God's help, and He will help you to correct your faults and you will enjoy His mercies.

8.2.4.en: (2) God's agreement to their request for a king (vv. 6-9:) 6 But the thing displeased Samuel, when they said, Give us a king to judge us. And Samuel prayed unto the LORD. 7 And the LORD said unto Samuel, Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them. 8 According to all the works which they have done since the day that I brought them up out of Egypt even unto this day, wherewith they have forsaken me, and served other gods, so do they also unto thee. 9 Now therefore hearken unto their voice: howbeit yet protest solemnly unto them, and shew them the manner of the king that shall reign over them.

8.3.0.en: The request of the leaders of the people seemed very ugly in Samuel's eyes .. Perhaps he felt an unexpected boldness from them, or that they were rejecting him after all these years of service, but because he was a spiritual man he found no way out for his bitter inner pains except prayer .. There is no rest except by opening the heart before God.

8.4.0.en: The Lord answered Samuel's prayer, and wanted to comfort him and soothe his heart, so He told him to grant the people their request to appoint an earthly king for them, and not to grieve himself, for this people had not rejected him but had rejected God, their true King. In real fatherhood, simplicity and humility from God, God likens Samuel to Himself and says to him that this people is difficult: after all that I did with them of great works, bringing them out of the land of Egypt, sustaining them and bringing them into the land of Canaan, they forsook Me and served Baal and the Ashtoreths, and as they have done to Me so they do to you also .. that is, you are like Me, O Samuel ..

8.4.1.en: Every priest, servant, father or mother learns from Samuel that the insult directed at him is directed at God, so he bears with those he shepherds in their faults, and that every honor directed to him is God's, so he gives thanks to Him.

8.5.0.en: And now, Samuel, respond to the people in their request to appoint a king for them, but before that you must tell them what will happen when a king is chosen, and what the results and consequences are that they did not study when they made that request, so that you will be innocent afterward of the results of their choice.

8.5.1.en: Here God allows them to appoint a king, and in His foreknowledge He knew that they would reject Him and ask for a king over them, so He declared this in the Law to Moses, and out of fatherly love He set conditions for this king so that he would not lead them away from God (Deut 17:14, 15). The conditions for this king are:

8.5.2.en: 1- God is the one who chooses him.

8.5.3.en: 2- He must be from the children of Israel and not a foreigner, lest he lead them astray to the worship of idols.

8.5.4.en: 3- He must not multiply horses, lest he become proud and enter into many wars that take him away from God and from care for his people, or return to Egypt to buy horses from it and so be tied to the worship of the Egyptian idols.

8.5.5.en: 4- He must not multiply wives, lest they turn his heart away from God.

8.5.6.en: 5- He must not greatly multiply silver and gold, lest he be proud of his wealth and be occupied with material things instead of God.

8.5.7.en: 6- He must write for himself a copy of the Law to read it always and act by it.

8.5.8.en: 7- The priest, as God's representative, anoints him.

8.5.9.en: 8- He has no right to perform the priestly service.

8.5.10.en: 9- God punishes him if he sins.

8.5.11.en: He is subject to God and has no absolute authority. As will appear in God's punishment of David at the numbering of the people...

8.5.12.en: In His foreknowledge God knew that they would ask for a king, so He laid down rules in His Law for the king to follow (Deut 17:

8.5.13.en: 14-20.) It is noted that the people asked for a king with the appearance of material power and not one who follows his heart after God, for they asked for a king to lead them in war and forgot that the true Leader who gives them victory is God, and that they had prevailed through the prayers of Samuel. The people forgot that God used to choose the judge in the age of the judges, whereas in the age of the monarchy the kingship is inherited by the son even if he is not suited to this office.

8.5.14.en: (3) The consequences of appointing a king (vv. 10-18:) 10 And Samuel told all the words of the LORD unto the people that asked of him a king. 11 And he said, This will be the manner of the king that shall reign over you: He will take your sons, and appoint them for himself, for his chariots, and to be his horsemen; and some shall run before his chariots. 12 And he will appoint him captains over thousands, and captains over fifties; and will set them to ear his ground, and to reap his harvest, and to make his instruments of war, and instruments of his chariots. 13 And he will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers. 14 And he will take your fields, and your vineyards, and your oliveyards, even the best of them, and give them to his servants. 15 And he will take the tenth of your seed, and of your vineyards, and give to his officers, and to his servants. 16 And he will take your menservants, and your maidservants, and your goodliest young men, and your asses, and put them to his work. 17 He will take the tenth of your sheep: and ye shall be his servants. 18 And ye shall cry out in that day because of your king which ye shall have chosen you; and the LORD will not hear you in that day.

8.6.0.en: Samuel gathered the leaders of the people and told them the word of God that He had spoken to him, which was that the people had rejected God, their King and Savior, and then he began to explain to them how it would be if an earthly king were chosen for them. The first thing is that this king will choose the best of their young men and make of them horsemen and slaves devoted to guarding him and driving his royal chariots, and some of them will have the task of running before the procession of his chariots in order to clear the way for him.

8.7.0.en: Likewise this king will appoint others whom he will make captains over fifties, hundreds and thousands to organize his service, that is, he will give them regular ranks as is customary in armies, and the task of these captains will be to oversee the plowing of his land and the harvesting of his crop, as well as the making of the instruments of war and the making of his own chariots.

8.8.0.en: Likewise also, he will take many of your daughters, and some of them will make perfumes and spices for his wives, and some will work in the royal kitchen as cooks, and the last as bakers. That is, whereas your daughters were free and honored in their parents' houses, they will become maidservants to the king.

8.9.0.en: Likewise he will take the best of your lands, and who will oppose a request of the king?

8.9.1.en: Or at least he may demand their produce to spend on his servants and soldiers who serve him, and whereas the tithes of the crops were given to the Levites, he will impose new tithes upon you (as a tax) to spend on his servants to ensure their loyalty and service to him.

8.10.0.en: And if he has need after that, he will dare more and more and will press your servants and animals into his service and the service of his house, his wives and his requirements, and no one will be able to say no to the king, even if he asks for your best and goodliest sons.

8.11.0.en: The taxes he imposes in the form of new tithes will not include only the agricultural crops, but will also include tithes of the sheep, as if the people were forced to pay two tenths of everything, one to God and the other to the new king. Besides this, the whole people will become slaves to him .. he commands and is obeyed, and presses them into all he wants, and no one can object; he permits whom he wishes and forbids whom he wills.

8.12.0.en: As a result of all the above, and with the increasing might of the king, you will murmur and then cry out because of what he inflicts on you, and your crying will increase and God will hear, but He will not answer, because you are the ones who chose this king in place of God.

8.12.1.en: Know that sin, however dazzling and pleasant it may seem, has its many troubles. So do not rush after your desires and personal opinions, but seek God and obey His commandments and you will live in security.

8.12.2.en: (4) The insistence on appointing a king (vv. 19-22:) 19 Nevertheless the people refused to obey the voice of Samuel; and they said, Nay; but we will have a king over us; 20 That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles. 21 And Samuel heard all the words of the people, and he rehearsed them in the ears of the LORD. 22 And the LORD said to Samuel, Hearken unto their voice, and make them a king. And Samuel said unto the men of Israel, Go ye every man unto his city.

8.13.0.en: Despite God's clear warning that Samuel spoke, the people refused to listen to the voice of wisdom, but increased in their demand and said with insistence: We must have a king and become a kingdom like the rest of the peoples around us who have kings .. and this king will have the awe of going out and coming in and leading the wars, and will also be the ruler and judge of all our problems and needs.

8.13.1.en: God, in His love and long-suffering, did not reject the people's request and gave them their freedom of choice, but He warned them of the results of appointing a king for them and they did not listen, so He allowed the appointment of the king as a kind of discipline for them for their insistence on their wrong request. God respects the freedom of your will, but may you seek His will, and so protect yourself. They chose a king with earthly, material qualifications and he wearied them, whereas Christ, the heavenly King, who reigns over the hearts of His children, gives them endless blessings and exploits them in nothing.

8.13.2.en: My God, You were the One who went out in the wars and led Your people, and You guided them through the judges, the prophets and the priests, but they rejected all that and asked for a king created from dust... How strange!!.. But I fear, my God, for myself... I fear that I may be like Your people and replace You with a king who reigns over my heart, a king whose name may be money, or another whose name is my mind and my thoughts... Do not allow it, my God, do not allow it, for I am afraid of myself.

8.14.0.en: Samuel heard from the people and returned to his prayer with God, and of course God was knowing and hearing, but this is the way of the faithful servants of God, who lift everything to God in their prayer. The Lord's answer to Samuel came clearly because He respects the will and freedom of man even in his betrayal of Him and departure from Him, and His answer was to appoint for them the king they asked for. With words like these Samuel spoke with the men and sent them away, each to his city.
